title: Trigonometric Integrals
body:
Integrals of powers and products of [[Trigonometric Function]]s: $\int \sin^m x\cos^n x\,dx$ and
$\int \tan^m x\sec^n x\,dx$. There is no new idea here, only bookkeeping: **peel off one factor so
the rest can be converted by an identity, then substitute.**

## Sine and cosine

| Case | Strategy |
|---|---|
| $\sin$ power **odd** | peel one $\sin x$ into $dx$, convert the rest with $\sin^2 = 1-\cos^2$, then $u = \cos x$ |
| $\cos$ power **odd** | peel one $\cos x$, convert with $\cos^2 = 1-\sin^2$, then $u = \sin x$ |
| both **even** | no factor to peel, so use the half-angle identities $\sin^2 x = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}$ and $\cos^2 x = \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}$ and repeat |

```
∫ sin³x cos²x dx        (sine odd)
  = ∫ sin²x cos²x · sin x dx
  = ∫ (1 − cos²x) cos²x · sin x dx      u = cos x,  du = −sin x dx
  = −∫ (1 − u²)u² du
  = −u³/3 + u⁵/5 + C
  = −cos³x/3 + cos⁵x/5 + C
```

The odd cases are one substitution. The both-even case is the tedious one, because the half-angle
identity has to be applied repeatedly and each pass only halves the power.

## Tangent and secant

Same idea, different pairing, because $\frac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^2 x$ and
$\frac{d}{dx}\sec x = \sec x\tan x$.

- $\sec$ power **even**: peel off $\sec^2 x$, convert the rest with $\sec^2 = 1+\tan^2$, take
  $u = \tan x$
- $\tan$ power **odd**: peel off $\sec x\tan x$, convert with $\tan^2 = \sec^2 - 1$, take
  $u = \sec x$
- neither: fall back on $\int \sec x\,dx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + C$, which is a memorised result,
  and reduction formulas from [[Integration By Parts]] for higher secant powers

$\int \sec^3 x\,dx$ is the standard nuisance: parts produces the original integral back, so you
solve for it algebraically, exactly the loop-closes case in [[Integration By Parts]].

## Products of different frequencies

$\int \sin mx\cos nx\,dx$ and friends are handled by the product-to-sum identities, which turn a
product into a sum of two ordinary sines or cosines. **These are the integrals that compute
[[Fourier Coefficients]]**, and the reason they mostly evaluate to zero is
[[Orthogonal Functions|orthogonality]]: distinct frequencies integrate to nothing over a full
period, which is what makes a [[Fourier Series]] decomposition possible at all.
